newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. envoy leaving Mideast, PLO-Israel stalemate.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy leaving Mideast, PLO-Israel stalemate.

text.p: U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross said he would leave the Middle East on Monday, having failed to break a stalemate in Israeli-PLO talks after 15 days of trying.
"I will be returning to the United States today and I will be consulting with the secretary of state," Ross told a news conference. He declined to discuss details of the negotiations.
He said there were still "delicate issues" to be negotiated.
The talks would continue without him and U.S. diplomats would take part, he said.
"I'm not giving details of the negotiations...We have made progress. We have made more progress in the security area than in the civilian affairs area," Ross said.

"There will be a continuing and active American role...I expect to return when I think the time is right and appropriate," he said. "My presence here isn't the determinant of whether you're going to have an agreement or not."
Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) negotiators said Ross's leaving did not reflect a crisis in the negotiations.

"I don't think Ross's departure is an attempt to apply pressure on the negotiators from both sides and it is not reflective of a crisis in the talks, which will continue," Palestinian negotiator Hassan Asfour told Reuters.

Ross said the sides would continue talks such as those held informally in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv and for the moment would not return to the Egyptian resort of Taba or the nearby Israeli vacation spot of Eilat.
Ross held the news conference at a Jerusalem hotel immediately after meeting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Netanyahu's office.
There was no immediate Israeli comment to Ross's decision.

Israel and the PLO are trying to clinch a deal to implement a long-promised partial Israeli troop pullback from Hebron, the last and most sensitive of seven West Bank cities due to be handed over to Palestinian rule in a 1995 peace accord.

West Bank and Gaza violence last month that claimed 60 Arab and 15 Israeli lives prompted U.S. President Bill Clinton to call a White House summit attended by Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and to send Ross to the region.
Ross said Washington would continue to be represented in the talks by U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk and U.S. Consul General in East Jerusalem Edward Abington.
The Hebron redeployment was to have occurred in March but was delayed after Islamic suicide bombers killed 59 people in Israel in February and March.
Netanyahu put the deal on hold demanding changes to enhance security for some 400 Jewish settlers who live amidst 100,000 Palestinians in Hebron.

Palestinians reject changes to the deal signed with Israel's previous government, ousted by Netanyahu in May elections. They say there is room in the existing deal for enhancing security arrangements.

Senior security PLO security official Mohammed Dahlan said the Palestinians would continue to oppose Israel's demands for changes including that Hebron police be armed only with pistols, that Israeli troops be allowed to chase wanted persons in PLO-controlled areas and for buffer zones.
